title: No Matter How Much: The Constitution of 2009

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *por más que* from B2 Unit 8: it means "however much" and takes the subjunctive when the amount or effort is open. *Por mucho que* and *por muy* + adjective + *que* work in the same way. When you tell something that really happened in the past, you may use the indicative. Here you use it for the Bolivian constitution of 2009 and the languages it recognises.

sections.title: However much…
rows: Por más que se hable castellano en las ciudades, los idiomas indígenas también son oficiales.
However much Spanish is spoken in the cities, the indigenous languages are official too.
Por más que se discuta, la wiphala es uno de los símbolos del Estado.
However much it is discussed, the wiphala is one of the symbols of the State.
Por muy antiguas que sean las costumbres de una comunidad, la Constitución las reconoce.
However old a community's customs are, the Constitution recognises them.
Por más que hubo desacuerdos, el texto se aprobó en un referéndum en enero de 2009.
Although there were disagreements, the text was approved in a referendum in January 2009. (it really happened: indicative)

items.spanish: Por más que se hable de la ley, mucha gente no conoce su texto.
items.english: However much the law is talked about, many people do not know its text.

items.spanish: Por mucho que cambie el gobierno, la Constitución sigue siendo la base del Estado.
items.english: However much the government changes, the Constitution remains the basis of the State.

items.spanish: Por más que lo pidieron, la asamblea no cambió ese artículo.
items.english: However much they asked for it, the assembly did not change that article.

sections.content: *Por más que* often comes with a main clause that says the result stays the same. For the future or for general statements use the subjunctive (*por más que se hable*); for a past event that really happened you may use the indicative (*por más que hubo*).
